nodes.explanation:
We prove that on the encoding of an evaluate-configuration whose program has constructor tag $k$ and payload $\mathit{body}$, `stepCostProg` returns whatever the $k$-th case program returns on the pair $(\mathit{body}, \mathit{env})$, with an additive overhead of $2\,\mathrm{size}(\mathit{body}) + 2\,\mathrm{size}(\mathit{env}) + \mathrm{size}(\mathit{kont}) + k + 14$.

The program `stepCostProg` is $\mathsf{elim}\,0\,\mathsf{nil}\,(\mathsf{elim}\,0\,\mathsf{nil}\,(\mathsf{elim}\,0\;\mathtt{stepCostEv}\;\mathtt{stepCostRet}))$: the first $\mathsf{elim}$ splits the configuration into control and (environment, stack), the second splits the control into its mode flag and the program, and the third tests the flag, which is $\mathsf{nil}$ for an evaluate-configuration, so it runs `stepCostEv`. That program is $\mathsf{elim}\,1\,\mathsf{nil}\,(\mathsf{let}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{var}\,1)\,(\mathtt{projLeft}\,5))\,(\mathtt{dispatch}\;\mathtt{costCases}\;1\;0))$: it splits the encoded program into its unary tag and payload, builds the pair of the payload (read by $\mathsf{var}\,1$, cost $\mathrm{size}(\mathit{body}) + 1$) and the encoded environment (the left component of the pair (environment, stack), obtained by `projLeft` at cost at most $\mathrm{size}(\mathit{env}) + \mathrm{size}(\mathit{kont}) + 3$), and then runs the dispatch chain with the tag at variable $1$ and the pair at variable $0$.

The proof constructs this derivation explicitly: four $\mathsf{elim}$ rules (one unit each), one $\mathsf{let}$ and one $\mathsf{cons}$ (one unit each), the two reads just described, and the dispatch. For the dispatch it invokes the imported theorem `dispatch_runs`: if variable $i$ holds the unary numeral $k$, variable $\mathit{idx}$ holds a value $p_k$, and the $k$-th program of the list runs on $[p_k]$ with result $r$ at cost $t$, then `dispatch` runs in the current environment with the same result at cost at most $t + \mathrm{size}(p_k) + k + 3$; the chain is a sequence of $\mathsf{elim}$s on the unary tag, each of which binds two more variables, which is why the index of the pair is adjusted by two per level and why the overhead grows with $k$. Here $p_k = \mathsf{cons}\;\mathit{body}\;\mathit{env}$ has size $\mathrm{size}(\mathit{body}) + \mathrm{size}(\mathit{env}) + 1$. Adding the contributions, $6 + (\mathrm{size}(\mathit{body}) + 1) + (\mathrm{size}(\mathit{env}) + \mathrm{size}(\mathit{kont}) + 3) + (t + \mathrm{size}(\mathit{body}) + \mathrm{size}(\mathit{env}) + 1 + k + 3)$, gives the stated bound.

nodes.theorem_title: The cost charged at a machine step is at most the size of the encoded configuration
nodes.natural_language_statement:
The evaluation machine of the ambient cost model charges, at each of its steps, the cost of the evaluation rule that the step implements: from a configuration $c$ in evaluation mode the charge $\mathsf{stepCost}(c)$ is $1 + \mathrm{size}(\rho(i))$ for a program $\mathsf{var}\,i$ (the value is copied), $\mathrm{size}(d)$ for $\mathsf{const}\,d$, $1$ for $\mathsf{nil}$, $\mathsf{cons}$, $\mathsf{elim}$ and $\mathsf{let}$, and $0$ for $\mathsf{loop}$; from a configuration in return mode it is $1$ when the top frame is a `loop1` frame (the loop rule is charged when the body's value is dispatched) and $0$ otherwise. Summing these charges along a run reproduces exactly the cost of the big-step derivation.

For every configuration $c$,
$$ \mathsf{stepCost}(c) \le \mathrm{size}(\lceil c\rceil) , $$
where $\lceil c\rceil$ is the data encoding `Cfg.toData c` of the configuration.

The lemma is a bookkeeping step of the clocked universal machine (blueprint `lem:universal-tm`): the clocked loop subtracts $\mathsf{stepCost}(c)$ from its remaining budget with the unary subtraction program, whose cost is quadratic in its arguments, and this inequality lets that cost be bounded in terms of the size guard $\Theta$ on configurations alone.

**Formalization Note**: `stepCost` is the function of `Cost/Machine.lean`; the encoding $\lceil c\rceil$ contains the encoded environment as a $\mathsf{cons}$-chain, so the size of any environment entry is dominated by it, and the program $\mathsf{const}\,d$ is encoded as $\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{ofNat}\,6)\,d$, so $\mathrm{size}(d)$ is dominated as well. The inequality holds with no hypothesis on $c$.

nodes.explanation:
We prove that $\mathsf{stepCost}(c) \le \mathrm{size}(\lceil c\rceil)$ for every configuration $c$ of the evaluation machine.

The proof is a case analysis on the control of $c$ and, in evaluation mode, on the constructor of the program; in return mode, on the stack. In every case except $\mathsf{var}$, the charged cost is $0$, $1$ or, for $\mathsf{const}\,d$, $\mathrm{size}(d)$, and the encoding $\lceil c\rceil = \mathsf{cons}\;\lceil\mathit{ctrl}\rceil\;(\mathsf{cons}\;\mathsf{list}(\rho)\;\mathsf{list}(\mathit{kont}))$ has size at least $3$, and in the $\mathsf{const}$ case at least $\mathrm{size}(d) + 1$ since the encoded program $\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{ofNat}\,6)\,d$ contains $d$; unfolding the sizes and a linear arithmetic check close these cases.

In the $\mathsf{var}\,i$ case the charge is $\mathrm{size}(\rho(i)) + 1$ where $\rho(i)$ is the value of variable $i$ (and $\mathsf{nil}$ if $i$ is out of range). The lemma `Data.getList_list` identifies $\rho(i)$ with the $i$-th element $\mathsf{getList}(\mathsf{list}\,\rho, i)$ of the encoded environment, and `size_getList_le` bounds the size of any element of a $\mathsf{cons}$-chain by the size of the chain, so $\mathrm{size}(\rho(i)) \le \mathrm{size}(\mathsf{list}\,\rho)$, and the encoded environment is a proper part of $\lceil c\rceil$, which has at least two further nodes.

nodes.theorem_title: `stepCostProg` computes the exact cost of a machine step, in time quadratic in the configuration size
nodes.natural_language_statement:
The evaluation machine of the ambient cost model charges at each step the cost $\mathsf{stepCost}(c)$ of the evaluation rule it implements ($1 + \mathrm{size}$ of the value read for a variable, $\mathrm{size}(d)$ for a literal $d$, one unit for $\mathsf{nil}$, $\mathsf{cons}$, $\mathsf{elim}$, $\mathsf{let}$ and for the dispatch of a loop body's value, and $0$ otherwise), so that the charges along a run add up to the cost of the big-step derivation. The clocked self-interpreter must decrement its cost budget by exactly this amount at each simulated step; `stepCostProg` is the fixed program of the model that computes it from the encoded configuration, returning it as a unary numeral $\mathsf{ofNat}(\cdot)$.

For every configuration $c$ there is a cost
$$ t \le \mathtt{stepCostBound}\bigl(\mathrm{size}(\lceil c\rceil)\bigr), \qquad \mathtt{stepCostBound}(S) = (S+1)(7S + 32) + 13S + 50, $$
such that `stepCostProg`, run on the single input $\lceil c\rceil$ (the encoding `Cfg.toData c`), halts with result
$$ \mathsf{ofNat}\bigl(\mathsf{stepCost}(c)\bigr) $$
at cost $t$.

The theorem is one of the two programs iterated by the clocked universal machine of blueprint `lem:universal-tm` (the other being the step program `stepProg`); its exactness is what makes the simulated budget agree with the true cost (`clockLoop_runs`, `clockRun_eq`), so that the clocked machine returns the result precisely when the simulated program halts within cost $k$.

**Formalization Note**: The bound is quadratic rather than linear because of the $\mathsf{var}$ case, where the value of variable $i$ is located by walking the encoded environment (`getListProg`, which copies the remainder of the environment at each of its steps) and its size is then computed in unary (`sizeProg`, quadratic in the size of the value). The constants of `stepCostBound` are those produced by the proof, with no attempt at optimality; only polynomiality matters downstream (`stepCostPoly`).
nodes.source: https://github.com/vidick/MIPRE-formalization/blob/70cbf1c52e3d5e1dff1162fdf952c9a9f4bd99ed/MIPRE/Foundations/Cost/Universal.lean#L576-L786; internal lemma of the formalization of blueprint lem:universal-tm, https://vidick.github.io/MIPRE-formalization/blueprint/
nodes.explanation:
We prove that `stepCostProg`, run on the encoding $\lceil c\rceil$ of a configuration $c$, returns the unary numeral $\mathsf{ofNat}(\mathsf{stepCost}(c))$ at cost at most $\mathtt{stepCostBound}(\mathrm{size}\lceil c\rceil) = (S+1)(7S+32) + 13S + 50$ with $S = \mathrm{size}\lceil c\rceil$.

The program first takes the configuration apart and branches on the mode of the control. On an evaluate-configuration it dispatches on the constructor tag of the program to one of seven case programs, each receiving the pair (payload, encoded environment); on a return-configuration it inspects the stack. The proof is a case analysis along the same lines: on the control, then on the seven program constructors or on the stack and its top frame.

Evaluate-configurations. Each of the seven cases is handled by the imported theorem `stepCostProg_ev`, which reduces a run of `stepCostProg` on the encoded configuration with tag $k$ and payload $\mathit{body}$ to a run of the $k$-th case program on the pair $(\mathit{body}, \mathit{env})$, at an additive overhead of $2\,\mathrm{size}(\mathit{body}) + 2\,\mathrm{size}(\mathit{env}) + \mathrm{size}(\mathit{kont}) + k + 14$. It remains to run the case programs. For $\mathsf{nil}$, $\mathsf{cons}$, $\mathsf{elim}$ and $\mathsf{let}$ (tags $1$ to $4$) the case program is the literal $\mathsf{const}(\mathsf{ofNat}\,1)$, which returns $\mathsf{ofNat}\,1$ at cost $3$; for $\mathsf{loop}$ (tag $5$) it is $\mathsf{nil}$, returning $\mathsf{nil} = \mathsf{ofNat}\,0$ at cost $1$. For $\mathsf{const}\,d$ (tag $6$) the case program `costConst` splits the pair and calls the unary size program `sizeProg` on $d$, which returns $\mathsf{ofNat}(\mathrm{size}\,d)$ at cost at most $(\mathrm{size}\,d + 1)(5\,\mathrm{size}\,d + 20) + \mathrm{size}\,d + 6$. For $\mathsf{var}\,i$ (tag $0$) the case program `costVar` builds the pair (encoded environment, $\mathsf{ofNat}\,i$) and calls the imported theorem `getListProg_runs`'s program `getListProg`, which returns the $i$-th element $w$ of the encoded environment at cost at most $(\mathrm{size}(\mathsf{ofNat}\,i) + 1)(\mathrm{size}(\mathsf{list}\,\rho) + \mathrm{size}(\mathsf{ofNat}\,i) + 12)$, then calls `sizeProg` on $w$ and finally prepends one $\mathsf{nil}$, obtaining $\mathsf{ofNat}(\mathrm{size}(w) + 1)$; by `Data.getList_list` the element $w$ is the value $\rho(i)$ of variable $i$, so this is the charged cost, and $\mathrm{size}(w) \le \mathrm{size}(\mathsf{list}\,\rho)$ (`size_getList_le`). In the two quadratic cases the costs are bounded in terms of a quantity $E \le S$ collecting the sizes of the components of the configuration, as $(E+1)(2E+12) + (E+1)(5E+20) = (E+1)(7E+32)$ plus linear terms, and `stepCostBound` is monotone (`stepCostBound_mono`), which gives the bound; in the constant cases the bound is immediate.

Return-configurations. Here `stepCostProg` runs `stepCostRet`, a chain of $\mathsf{elim}$s that reads the stack and, if non-empty, the unary tag of its top frame. On an empty stack and on the frames `cons1`, `cons2`, `let1` (tags $0$, $1$, $2$) it returns $\mathsf{nil} = \mathsf{ofNat}\,0$, and on a `loop1` frame (tag $3$) it returns $\mathsf{const}(\mathsf{ofNat}\,1)$; each of these runs is written out explicitly, costs a constant below $50$, and matches the definition of $\mathsf{stepCost}$ in return mode.

nodes.theorem_title: One iteration of the clocked loop, first half: finality test, step cost and budget subtraction
nodes.natural_language_statement:
The clocked self-interpreter runs the evaluation machine under a cost budget. Its loop state is $\mathtt{clockState}(d, \mathit{rem}, \mathit{bud}, \theta) = \mathsf{cons}\,d\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathit{rem}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathit{bud}\,\theta))$: the encoded configuration $d$, the remaining cost budget, the remaining step budget and the size guard, the last three as unary numerals. The loop body `clockBody` tests whether the configuration is final and otherwise, if the step budget is positive, computes the cost of the next step with `stepCostProg`, subtracts it from the remaining cost budget with the unary subtraction `subProg`, and then runs the second half `clockRest` (perform the step, compare the new configuration's size with the guard, and continue or stop). Let $\mathtt{clockEnv}(c, \mathit{rem}, b, \Theta, \rho)$ denote the environment reached at that point: on top of the loop state and the intermediate values it holds the pair $(\mathsf{ofNat}(\mathsf{stepCost}\,c), \mathsf{ofNat}\,\mathit{rem})$ and, at variable $0$, the value $\mathtt{subResult}(\mathsf{stepCost}\,c, \mathit{rem})$ of the subtraction (the flagged difference, or $\mathsf{nil}$ when the step cost exceeds the remaining budget).

Let $c$ be a configuration that is not final, let $\mathit{rem}, b, \Theta \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\rho$ be an environment, $r$ a value and $t \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose that the remainder of the body, the program $\mathsf{elim}\,0\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,\mathtt{clockRest}$ which stops with $\mathsf{nil}$ if the subtraction failed and otherwise runs `clockRest`, halts in the environment $\mathtt{clockEnv}(c, \mathit{rem}, b, \Theta, \rho)$ with result $r$ at cost $t$. Then there is a cost
$$ s \le t + \mathtt{stepCostBound}\bigl(\mathrm{size}\lceil c\rceil\bigr) + \mathtt{subBound}\bigl(\mathsf{stepCost}(c), \mathit{rem}\bigr) + 4\,\mathrm{size}\lceil c\rceil + 4\,\mathit{rem} + 30 $$
such that `clockBody` halts in the environment $\mathtt{clockState}(\lceil c\rceil, \mathsf{ofNat}\,\mathit{rem}, \mathsf{ofNat}(b+1), \mathsf{ofNat}\,\Theta) :: \rho$ with the same result $r$ at cost $s$. Here $\mathtt{stepCostBound}(S) = (S+1)(7S+32) + 13S + 50$ and $\mathtt{subBound}(a, b) = (a+1)(2a+2b+14)$.

The lemma is the common prefix of the three outcomes of a non-final iteration with positive step budget in the correctness proof of the clocked loop (`clockLoop_runs`): continue with the stepped configuration, stop because the guard is exceeded, or stop because the step cost exceeds the remaining budget. It serves the clocked universal machine of blueprint `lem:universal-tm`.

**Formalization Note**: The step budget is written $b + 1$ because the body's first action on a non-final configuration is to test it against $\mathsf{nil}$ (the exhausted-budget case is `clockBody_budget0`). `clockEnv` is the explicit twelve-entry environment of `Cost/Universal.lean`; the statement is a cost transfer from the second half to the whole body, with $r$ and the hypothesis run arbitrary.
nodes.source: https://github.com/vidick/MIPRE-formalization/blob/70cbf1c52e3d5e1dff1162fdf952c9a9f4bd99ed/MIPRE/Foundations/Cost/Universal.lean#L898-L926; internal lemma of the formalization of blueprint lem:universal-tm, https://vidick.github.io/MIPRE-formalization/blueprint/
nodes.explanation:
We prove that a run of the second half of the clocked loop body, from the environment $\mathtt{clockEnv}(c, \mathit{rem}, b, \Theta, \rho)$ with result $r$ at cost $t$, extends to a run of the whole body `clockBody` from the loop state $(\lceil c\rceil, \mathsf{ofNat}\,\mathit{rem}, \mathsf{ofNat}(b+1), \mathsf{ofNat}\,\Theta)$ with the same result, at an additional cost of at most $\mathtt{stepCostBound}(S) + \mathtt{subBound}(\mathsf{stepCost}\,c, \mathit{rem}) + 4S + 4\,\mathit{rem} + 30$, where $S = \mathrm{size}\lceil c\rceil$ and $c$ is not final.

The body is $\mathsf{elim}\,0\,\mathsf{nil}\,(\mathsf{elim}\,1\,\mathsf{nil}\,(\mathsf{elim}\,1\,\mathsf{nil}\,(\mathsf{let}\,(\mathtt{callVar}\,4\;\mathtt{isFinalProg})\,(\mathsf{elim}\,0\;\mathtt{clockStep}\;\ldots))))$, and `clockStep` is $\mathsf{elim}\,1\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,(\mathsf{let}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathtt{callVar}\,7\;\mathtt{stepCostProg})\,(\mathsf{var}\,5))\,(\mathsf{let}\,(\mathtt{callVar}\,0\;\mathtt{subProg})\,(\mathsf{elim}\,0\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,\mathtt{clockRest})))$. The proof writes out the derivation of the body up to the hypothesis run, rule by rule, and then bounds its cost.

The three $\mathsf{elim}$s unpack the state into the configuration, the remaining cost, the step budget and the guard (one unit each). `callVar 4 isFinalProg` copies the configuration (cost $S + 1$) and runs the finality test on it; since $c$ is not final, `isFinalProg_nonfinal` gives the value $\mathsf{nil}$ at cost at most $8$, so the following $\mathsf{elim}$ takes its $\mathsf{nil}$ branch into `clockStep`. There, the step budget $\mathsf{ofNat}(b+1) = \mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,(\mathsf{ofNat}\,b)$ is a $\mathsf{cons}$, so the $\mathsf{elim}$ continues. The pair for the subtraction is built from `callVar 7 stepCostProg`, which copies the configuration ($S+1$) and runs the step-cost program, and from $\mathsf{var}\,5$, which reads $\mathsf{ofNat}\,\mathit{rem}$ (cost $2\,\mathit{rem} + 2$). The imported theorem `stepCostProg_runs` asserts that the step-cost program returns $\mathsf{ofNat}(\mathsf{stepCost}\,c)$ at cost at most $\mathtt{stepCostBound}(S)$. Then `callVar 0 subProg` copies the pair (cost $2\,\mathsf{stepCost}(c) + 2\,\mathit{rem} + 4$) and runs the subtraction; the imported theorem `subProg_runs` asserts that it returns $\mathtt{subResult}(\mathsf{stepCost}\,c, \mathit{rem})$ at cost at most $\mathtt{subBound}(\mathsf{stepCost}\,c, \mathit{rem})$. The environment at this point is exactly $\mathtt{clockEnv}(c, \mathit{rem}, b, \Theta, \rho)$, so the hypothesis run completes the derivation of the $\mathsf{let}$.

Adding the costs gives $t + \mathtt{stepCostBound}(S) + \mathtt{subBound}(\mathsf{stepCost}\,c, \mathit{rem}) + 2S + 2\,\mathsf{stepCost}(c) + 4\,\mathit{rem}$ plus a constant below $30$; the imported theorem `stepCost_le_size`, $\mathsf{stepCost}(c) \le S$, turns the term $2\,\mathsf{stepCost}(c)$ into $2S$, which yields the stated bound.

nodes.theorem_title: The clocked loop computes `clockRun` at cost $(b+1)(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta,k)+1)$ for step budget $b$
nodes.natural_language_statement:
The clocked self-interpreter runs the evaluation machine from a configuration $c_0$ under three guards: a cost budget $k$ (the cumulative cost $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n)$ of the first $n$ steps, which is the sum of the charges $\mathsf{stepCost}$ along the run, may not exceed $k$), a step budget $b$ (at most $b$ further iterations), and a size guard $\Theta$ (the encoded size of every configuration handled may not exceed $\Theta$). Its loop state is $\mathtt{clockState}(\lceil c\rceil, \mathsf{ofNat}\,\mathit{rem}, \mathsf{ofNat}\,b, \mathsf{ofNat}\,\Theta)$, where $\mathit{rem}$ is the remaining cost budget, and the body `clockBody` stops with the flagged value $\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,r$ on a final configuration with value $r$, stops with $\mathsf{nil}$ when the step budget is exhausted, when the next step costs more than the remaining budget, or when the next configuration exceeds the guard, and otherwise continues with the stepped configuration, the decremented budgets and the same guard.

The intended value of the loop is the function $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n)$, defined by recursion on $b$: if the $n$-th configuration $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)$ is final it is the flagged value of that configuration; otherwise, if $b = 0$ it is $\mathsf{nil}$, and if $b = b' + 1$ it is $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b', n+1)$ when $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1) \le k$ and $\mathrm{size}\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n+1}(c_0)\rceil \le \Theta$, and $\mathsf{nil}$ otherwise.

Let $c_0$ be a configuration, $k, \Theta \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\rho$ an environment. For all $b, n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
1. $b \le 3k + 1$,
2. $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n) \le k$, and
3. $\mathrm{size}\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)\rceil \le \Theta$,

there is a cost
$$ t \le (b+1)\bigl(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, k) + 1\bigr) $$
such that $\mathsf{loop}\;\mathtt{clockBody}$, evaluated in the environment $\mathtt{clockState}\bigl(\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)\rceil, \mathsf{ofNat}(k - \mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n)), \mathsf{ofNat}\,b, \mathsf{ofNat}\,\Theta\bigr) :: \rho$, halts with result $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n)$ at cost $t$. Here
$$ \mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, k) = \mathtt{stepCostBound}(\Theta) + \mathtt{subBound}(\Theta, k) + \mathtt{stepBound}(\Theta) + \mathtt{sizeBound}(\mathtt{stepBound}\,\Theta) + \mathtt{subBound}(\mathtt{stepBound}\,\Theta, \Theta) + 6\,\mathtt{stepBound}(\Theta) + 12\Theta + 30k + 200 , $$
a polynomial in $\Theta$ and $k$ (with $\mathtt{stepBound}(S) = (S+1)(S+40)+200$, $\mathtt{stepCostBound}(S) = (S+1)(7S+32)+13S+50$, $\mathtt{subBound}(a,b) = (a+1)(2a+2b+14)$ and $\mathtt{sizeBound}(s) = (s+1)(5s+20)+s+6$).

This is the core of the clocked universal machine of blueprint `lem:universal-tm`: `univTProg_runs` applies it from the initial configuration with $n = 0$ and $b = 3k+1$, and identifies $\mathtt{clockRun}$ with the budgeted result `clockedResult` (`clockRun_eq`, from `clockRun_of_final` and `clockRun_of_not`). The bound shows that the loop costs at most polynomially in $k$ and $\Theta$ whether or not the simulated run halts.

**Formalization Note**: The remaining cost budget in the state is the truncated difference $k - \mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n)$, which hypothesis 2 makes an honest difference; the condition $b \le 3k+1$ is only used to bound the cost of reading the step budget. `clockRun` is a noncomputable definition (it decides finality classically) used purely as a specification. All numerals in the state are unary.
nodes.source: https://github.com/vidick/MIPRE-formalization/blob/70cbf1c52e3d5e1dff1162fdf952c9a9f4bd99ed/MIPRE/Foundations/Cost/Universal.lean#L1031-L1105; internal lemma of the formalization of blueprint lem:universal-tm, https://vidick.github.io/MIPRE-formalization/blueprint/
nodes.explanation:
We prove that the clocked loop, started on the state $(\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)\rceil, \mathsf{ofNat}(k - \mathsf{costSum}(c_0,n)), \mathsf{ofNat}\,b, \mathsf{ofNat}\,\Theta)$ under the hypotheses $b \le 3k+1$, $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n) \le k$ and $\mathrm{size}\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)\rceil \le \Theta$, halts with result $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n)$ at cost at most $(b+1)(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta,k)+1)$.

The proof is an induction on the step budget $b$, for all $n$, mirroring the recursion that defines $\mathtt{clockRun}$. Each case constructs one iteration of the body from lemmas about its parts and applies a $\mathsf{loop}$ rule; the lemma `clockBody_cost_le` then shows that one non-final iteration costs at most $\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, k)$, using that the configuration size $S$ is at most $\Theta$, the remaining budget at most $k$, the step cost at most $S$, and the monotonicity of all the component bounds.

Base case $b = 0$. If $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)$ is final with value $r$, `clockBody_final` gives a body run returning the stop signal with the flagged value at cost at most $3\Theta + 30$, and the stopping rule gives the loop run; this matches $\mathtt{clockRun}$. Otherwise `clockBody_budget0` gives a body run on an exhausted step budget returning the stop signal with $\mathsf{nil}$ at cost at most $\Theta + 20$, again matching $\mathtt{clockRun}$.

Inductive step $b + 1$. The final case is as before. For a non-final configuration $c = \mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)$ there are three sub-cases, following the definition of $\mathtt{clockRun}$. The imported theorem `stepCost_le_size` provides $\mathsf{stepCost}(c) \le \mathrm{size}\lceil c\rceil \le \Theta$ throughout. (i) If $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1) \le k$ and $\mathrm{size}\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n+1}(c_0)\rceil \le \Theta$: by `costSum_succ`, $\mathsf{stepCost}(c) \le k - \mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n)$, so the subtraction succeeds; `clockRest_continue` runs the second half of the body, which performs the step with the step program (imported theorem `stepProg_runs`: `stepProg` returns $\lceil\mathsf{step}(c)\rceil$ at cost at most $\mathtt{stepBound}(\mathrm{size}\lceil c\rceil)$), computes the new configuration's size in unary and compares it with the guard by the unary subtraction (imported theorem `subProg_runs`), and returns the continue signal with the new state, whose remaining budget is $k - \mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1)$; the imported theorem `clockBody_prefix` extends this to a run of the whole body; the induction hypothesis at $n+1$ gives the rest of the loop with value $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n+1)$, and the continuing rule assembles the run, at cost at most $\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, k) + (b+1)(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta,k)+1) + 1 = (b+2)(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta,k)+1)$. (ii) If the cost condition holds but the new configuration exceeds the guard, `clockRest_stop` runs the second half to the stop signal with $\mathsf{nil}$, `clockBody_prefix` extends it, and the stopping rule finishes; $\mathtt{clockRun}$ is $\mathsf{nil}$ here. (iii) If $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1) > k$, then $\mathsf{stepCost}(c)$ exceeds the remaining budget, the subtraction returns $\mathsf{nil}$, and the $\mathsf{elim}$ guarding `clockRest` returns the stop signal with $\mathsf{nil}$ directly; `clockBody_prefix` and the stopping rule finish, again with value $\mathsf{nil}$ as $\mathtt{clockRun}$ prescribes. In (ii) and (iii) the cost is one iteration plus one unit, within the bound.

nodes.theorem_title: `clockRun` returns the flagged value on a run that halts within the cost budget and the size guard
nodes.natural_language_statement:
Let $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n)$ be the specification of the clocked interpreter loop: starting from the $n$-th configuration $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)$ of the machine run of $c_0$, with $b$ further iterations allowed, it is the flagged value $\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,r$ if the current configuration is final with value $r$; otherwise it is $\mathsf{nil}$ if $b = 0$, and for $b = b'+1$ it is $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b', n+1)$ when the cumulative cost $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1)$ of the first $n+1$ steps is at most $k$ and the encoded size of the $(n+1)$-st configuration is at most $\Theta$, and $\mathsf{nil}$ otherwise.

Let $c_0$ be a configuration, $k, \Theta, N \in \mathbb{N}$, $r$ a value and $e$ an environment. Suppose that
1. $\mathsf{step}^{N}(c_0) = \langle\mathsf{ret}\,r, e, [\,]\rangle$ (the run reaches a final configuration with value $r$ at step $N$),
2. $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, N) \le k$ (it does so within the cost budget), and
3. $\mathrm{size}\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)\rceil \le \Theta$ for all $n$ (every configuration of the run is within the guard).

Then for all $b, n$ with $n \le N \le n + b$,
$$ \mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n) = \mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,r . $$

Together with `clockRun_of_not` (the timeout case) this identifies the value of the clocked loop with the budgeted result `clockedResult` (`clockRun_eq`): a run of cost $t \le k$ takes at most $3t \le 3k$ machine steps (`eval_steps_count`), so the step budget $3k+1$ suffices. It serves the clocked universal machine of blueprint `lem:universal-tm`.

**Formalization Note**: `clockRun` is the noncomputable specification function of `Cost/Universal.lean` (finality is decided classically); the statement is purely about it and the machine, not about any program. Hypothesis 3 is demanded for all $n$, which is harmless since final configurations are fixed. The conclusion holds for every $n \le N$, not only $n = 0$, as required by the induction.

nodes.explanation:
We prove that if the machine run of $c_0$ reaches the final configuration $\langle\mathsf{ret}\,r, e, [\,]\rangle$ at step $N$ with $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, N) \le k$ and all configurations within the guard $\Theta$, then $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n)$ is the flagged value of $r$ whenever $n \le N \le n + b$.

The proof is an induction on the step budget $b$, for all $n$. In the base case $b = 0$ the hypotheses force $n = N$, the $n$-th configuration is the final one, and $\mathtt{clockRun}$ returns the flagged value of its $\mathsf{val}$, which is $r$.

For $b + 1$, first suppose that $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)$ is already final, with some value $r'$ and environment $e'$. Final configurations are fixed by the step function (`step_final`), so $\mathsf{step}^{N}(c_0) = \mathsf{step}^{N-n}(\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)) = \langle\mathsf{ret}\,r', e', [\,]\rangle$, and comparing with hypothesis 1 gives $r' = r$; $\mathtt{clockRun}$ returns the flagged value of $r$. Otherwise $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)$ is not final, which forces $n < N$: if $n \ge N$ then $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0) = \mathsf{step}^{n-N}(\mathsf{step}^{N}(c_0))$ would be the fixed final configuration. Since $n + 1 \le N$, the cumulative cost is monotone in the number of steps (`costSum_le_of_le`), so $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1) \le \mathsf{costSum}(c_0, N) \le k$, and hypothesis 3 gives the guard condition at $n+1$; hence $\mathtt{clockRun}$ recurses to $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n+1)$, and the induction hypothesis applies because $n + 1 \le N \le (n+1) + b$.

nodes.theorem_title: `clockRun` returns the timeout value $\mathsf{nil}$ when the program does not halt within the cost budget
nodes.natural_language_statement:
Let $c$ be a program of the ambient cost model and $v$ an input, and let $c_0 = \langle\mathsf{ev}\,c, [v], [\,]\rangle$ be the initial configuration of the evaluation machine for $c$ on $v$. Let $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n)$ be the specification of the clocked interpreter loop started on the $n$-th configuration of the run with $b$ further iterations, cost budget $k$ and size guard $\Theta$: it is the flagged value of the current configuration if that is final, and otherwise either $\mathsf{nil}$ (when $b = 0$, when the cumulative cost $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1)$ would exceed $k$, or when the next configuration exceeds the guard) or the value at the next configuration with one fewer iteration.

Suppose that $c$ does not halt on $v$ within cost $k$: there are no $r$ and $t \le k$ with $\mathsf{Eval}\;[v]\;c\;r\;t$. Then for all $b, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n) \le k$,
$$ \mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n) = \mathsf{nil} . $$

This is the timeout half of the identification of the clocked loop's value with the budgeted result `clockedResult` (`clockRun_eq`; the other half is `clockRun_of_final`), used by the clocked universal machine of blueprint `lem:universal-tm`.

**Formalization Note**: The hypothesis is stated with `Prog.Runs c v r t`, that is, a derivation in the one-element environment $[v]$, and the cost $k$ is the cost of the big-step semantics, not a number of machine steps. The guard $\Theta$ plays no role in the conclusion. The condition $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n) \le k$ is what the recursion of `clockRun` maintains; at $n = 0$ it is trivial.
nodes.source: https://github.com/vidick/MIPRE-formalization/blob/70cbf1c52e3d5e1dff1162fdf952c9a9f4bd99ed/MIPRE/Foundations/Cost/Universal.lean#L1138-L1157; internal lemma of the formalization of blueprint lem:universal-tm, https://vidick.github.io/MIPRE-formalization/blueprint/
nodes.explanation:
We prove that if the program $c$ has no run on $v$ of cost at most $k$, then $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n) = \mathsf{nil}$ for every step budget $b$ and every $n$ with $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n) \le k$, where $c_0$ is the initial configuration of $c$ on $v$.

The key observation is that no configuration reached within the cost budget is final. Suppose $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0) = \langle\mathsf{ret}\,r, e, [\,]\rangle$ with $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n) \le k$. The imported theorem `eval_of_steps` asserts that a machine run from $\langle\mathsf{ev}\,p, \rho, \kappa\rangle$ that reaches a final configuration in $n$ steps contains a derivation $\mathsf{Eval}\;\rho\;p\;r'\;t'$ whose machine run has $M \le n$ steps, reaches $\langle\mathsf{ret}\,r', e', \kappa\rangle$ and accumulates cost exactly $t'$. Applied with $p = c$, $\rho = [v]$ and the empty stack, it yields a run of $c$ on $v$ with result $r'$ and cost $t' = \mathsf{costSum}(c_0, M)$; since the cumulative cost is monotone in the number of steps (`costSum_le_of_le`) and $M \le n$, we get $t' \le \mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n) \le k$, contradicting the hypothesis.

With this, the claim follows by induction on $b$. For $b = 0$ the configuration $\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)$ is not final, so $\mathtt{clockRun}$ is $\mathsf{nil}$ by definition. For $b + 1$ the configuration is again not final; if the recursion condition holds, in particular $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, n+1) \le k$, the value is $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, b, n+1)$, which is $\mathsf{nil}$ by the induction hypothesis, and otherwise the value is $\mathsf{nil}$ directly.

nodes.theorem_title: The clocked universal program returns the budgeted result `clockedResult c v k` in time polynomial in $k + |c| + |v|$
nodes.natural_language_statement:
Fix the ambient cost model: programs $c \in \mathsf{Prog}$ act on values $v \in \mathsf{Data}$ (binary trees), $\mathsf{Eval}\;[v]\;c\;r\;t$ (in Lean `c.Runs v r t`) says that $c$ on input $v$ halts with result $r$ at cost $t$, every program is encoded as a value $\lceil c\rceil$ (`encode c`, the tree encoding `Prog.toData`) of size $|c| = \mathrm{esize}(c)$, and natural numbers used as budgets are passed in unary, $\mathsf{ofNat}(k)$ being the list of $k$ copies of $\mathsf{nil}$. The *budgeted result* of $c$ on $v$ under the cost budget $k$ is
$$ \mathtt{clockedResult}(c, v, k) = \begin{cases} \mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,r & \text{if } c \text{ halts on } v \text{ with result } r \text{ at some cost } t \le k, \\ \mathsf{nil} & \text{otherwise (timeout)}, \end{cases} $$
which is well defined because the semantics is deterministic.

`univTProg` is a fixed closed program, the clocked self-interpreter: on the input $(\mathsf{ofNat}\,k, (\lceil c\rceil, v))$ it computes $X = k + |c| + |v|$ and a size guard $\Theta(X)$ in unary, builds the initial configuration of the evaluation machine for $c$ on $v$, and runs the clocked interpreter loop with cost budget $k$, step budget $3k+1$ and guard $\Theta(X)$. The theorem states its correctness and its time bound.

For every program $c$, every value $v$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a cost
$$ t \le \mathtt{univTBoundFun}(k + |c| + |v|) $$
such that `univTProg`, run on the single input $\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{ofNat}\,k)\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v)$, halts with result $\mathtt{clockedResult}(c, v, k)$ at cost $t$. The function $\mathtt{univTBoundFun}$ is an explicit polynomial (`univTPoly`): with $Y(X) = 9X + 4$, $T_1(X) = Y(2Y+2) + 1$ and $\Theta(X) = Y(T_1 + 1) + 1$,
$$ \mathtt{univTBoundFun}(X) = 2\,\mathtt{sizeBound}(X) + 2\,\mathtt{addBound}(X,X) + 2\,\mathtt{tripleBound}(X,1) + \mathtt{tripleBound}(3X+1,1) + \mathtt{repBound}(Y, 2Y+1, 1) + \mathtt{repBound}(Y, T_1, 1) + \mathtt{sizeBound}(\Theta) + (3X+2)\bigl(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, X) + 1\bigr) + 20\Theta + 20T_1 + 60Y + 100X + 500 , $$
where $\mathtt{sizeBound}$, $\mathtt{addBound}$, $\mathtt{tripleBound}$, $\mathtt{repBound}$ are the (quadratic) cost bounds of the unary size, addition, tripling and replication programs and $\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, k)$ is the polynomial cost bound of one iteration of the clocked loop.

This theorem is the `run` field of the clocked universal machine `selfClockedUniversal`, and so proves `exists_clocked_universal`, half of blueprint `lem:universal-tm` ([MNY, Lemma 2.1]). The clocked machine is the primitive with which the deciders of the compression pipeline simulate other deciders under a budget, and with which the recursive compression argument runs a description "for $\log n$ steps".

**Formalization Note**: The budget $k$ counts cost units of the big-step semantics (not machine steps), is supplied in unary (so the input has size $2k + 1 + |c| + |v| + 2$), and the bound is polynomial in $k$ itself. The result is total: the program halts on every input, also when the simulated run does not halt, which is what the step budget $3k+1$ and the size guard $\Theta$ are for; the guard never fires on a run that halts within the budget, whose configurations have size at most $\mathtt{sigmaFun}(X) \le \Theta(X)$. The constants in the bound are those produced by the proof.
nodes.source: https://github.com/vidick/MIPRE-formalization/blob/70cbf1c52e3d5e1dff1162fdf952c9a9f4bd99ed/MIPRE/Foundations/Cost/Universal.lean#L1251-L1407; internal lemma of the formalization of blueprint lem:universal-tm, https://vidick.github.io/MIPRE-formalization/blueprint/
nodes.explanation:
We prove that the clocked self-interpreter `univTProg`, on the input $(\mathsf{ofNat}\,k, (\lceil c\rceil, v))$, returns $\mathtt{clockedResult}(c, v, k)$ at cost at most $\mathtt{univTBoundFun}(X)$, $X = k + |c| + |v|$.

The proof has three parts: the prelude that computes the guard and assembles the loop state, the loop, and the identification of the loop's value with the budgeted result; each part also contributes its cost. The prelude is a sequence of $\mathsf{let}$ bindings calling closed unary-arithmetic programs through `callVar` (copy the argument, then run the program on it). It computes $\mathsf{ofNat}\,|c|$ and $\mathsf{ofNat}\,|v|$ with `sizeProg`, adds them and then $k$ with `addProg` to obtain $\mathsf{ofNat}\,X$, applies `tripleProg` twice ($n, m \mapsto 3n + m$) to obtain $\mathsf{ofNat}(3X+1)$ and $\mathsf{ofNat}\,Y$ with $Y = 3(3X+1)+1 = 9X+4$, and builds with `repProg` a list of $Y$ copies of a list of $Y$ copies of $\mathsf{ofNat}\,Y$, whose size, computed by `sizeProg`, is $\Theta = Y(Y(2Y+2)+2) + 1 = \mathtt{thetaFun}(X)$ in unary (`size_list_replicate`). It then builds the encoded initial configuration $\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\lceil c\rceil)\,(\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,v\,\mathsf{nil})\,\mathsf{nil}) = \lceil\langle\mathsf{ev}\,c, [v], [\,]\rangle\rceil$, computes $\mathsf{ofNat}(3k+1)$ with one more `tripleProg`, and assembles the state $(\lceil c_0\rceil, \mathsf{ofNat}\,k, \mathsf{ofNat}(3k+1), \mathsf{ofNat}\,\Theta)$ on which it runs $\mathsf{loop}\;\mathtt{clockBody}$. Each of these programs has a cost lemma, and the whole derivation is written out.

For the loop, the imported theorem `clockLoop_runs` is applied with $c_0 = \langle\mathsf{ev}\,c, [v], [\,]\rangle$, $n = 0$ and step budget $b = 3k + 1$: its hypotheses hold since $\mathsf{costSum}(c_0, 0) = 0 \le k$ and the initial configuration has size at most $|c| + |v| + 7 \le Y \le \Theta$. It yields a run of the loop with value $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, 3k+1, 0)$ at cost at most $(3k+2)(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, k) + 1)$, which is at most $(3X+2)(\mathtt{clockBodyBound}(\Theta, X) + 1)$ by monotonicity in the budget.

The identification $\mathtt{clockRun}(c_0, k, \Theta, 3k+1, 0) = \mathtt{clockedResult}(c, v, k)$ is the lemma `clockRun_eq`, whose hypothesis is that the guard dominates every configuration of any run of $c$ on $v$ of cost $t \le k$. The initial configuration satisfies $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,X\,X\,X\,X$ (no returned value, program size $|c| \le X$, one environment entry of size $|v| \le X$, empty stack). The imported theorem `eval_steps_bound` (in its `eval_steps_bound_forever` form, which extends it past the final configuration using that final configurations are fixed) asserts that along the machine run simulating a derivation of cost $t \le V$ from a configuration satisfying $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,V\,L\,P\,K$, every configuration satisfies $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,V\,(L+2t)\,P\,(K+t)$; with $t \le k \le X$ this gives $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,X\,(3X)\,X\,(2X)$ after weakening, and the imported theorem `size_toData_le` bounds the encoded size of such a configuration by $\mathtt{cfgSizeBound}(X, 3X, X, 2X) = \mathtt{sigmaFun}(X)$, a polynomial of degree three, which is at most $\Theta(X)$ (`sigmaFun_le_thetaFun`). Given this, `clockRun_eq` distinguishes two cases. If some run of $c$ on $v$ has cost $t \le k$, the imported theorem `eval_steps_count` provides a machine run of $N \le 3t \le 3k$ steps reaching the final configuration with the run's result and accumulated cost exactly $t \le k$, and the imported theorem `clockRun_of_final` (the flagged value is returned when the run halts within the cost budget and the guard in at most $b$ steps, here $N \le 3k+1$) gives the flagged result, which is $\mathtt{clockedResult}$ by the definition of `evalWithin`. Otherwise the imported theorem `clockRun_of_not` gives $\mathsf{nil}$, which is again $\mathtt{clockedResult}$.

Finally the cost: each prelude program is bounded by its cost lemma, made monotone in $|c|, |v|, k \le X$ (two $\mathtt{sizeBound}(X)$ terms, two $\mathtt{addBound}(X,X)$, three $\mathtt{tripleBound}$ terms, the two $\mathtt{repBound}$ terms and $\mathtt{sizeBound}(\Theta)$), and the reads and copies of the intermediate unary values are bounded by the linear terms $20\Theta + 20T_1 + 60Y + 100X + 500$; the sum is $\mathtt{univTBoundFun}(X)$.

nodes.theorem_title: Existence of an efficient universal machine for the ambient cost model
nodes.natural_language_statement:
Fix the ambient cost model of the formalization: programs $c \in \mathsf{Prog}$ run on values $v \in \mathsf{Data}$ (binary trees), $\mathsf{Eval}\;[v]\;c\;r\;t$ (in Lean `c.Runs v r t`) says that $c$ on input $v$ halts with result $r$ at cost $t \in \mathbb{N}$, so that $\varphi_c(v) = r$ for the unique such $r$, and $\mathrm{runtime}(c, v) = t$; every program is encoded as a value $\lceil c\rceil$ (`encode c`, the tree serialization `Prog.toData`) of size $|c| = \mathrm{esize}(c)$, and pairs are encoded by $\mathsf{cons}$. A program is *closed* (`WellScoped 1`) when it reads only its input, variable $0$.

An *efficient universal machine* (`UniversalMachine`) is a structure consisting of a closed program $u$ and a polynomial $p \in \mathbb{N}[X]$ such that:
1. (simulation, with time bound) for every program $c$, input $v$, result $r$ and cost $t$ with $\mathsf{Eval}\;[v]\;c\;r\;t$, there is a cost $t' \le p\bigl(|c| + |v| + t\bigr)$ with $\mathsf{Eval}\;[\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v]\;u\;r\;t'$;
2. (no spurious halting) for every $c$, $v$, $r$ and $t'$ with $\mathsf{Eval}\;[\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v]\;u\;r\;t'$, there is a cost $t$ with $\mathsf{Eval}\;[v]\;c\;r\;t$.

The theorem states that such a machine exists:
$$ \mathsf{Nonempty}\;\mathtt{UniversalMachine} , $$
that is, there are a closed program $u$ and a polynomial $p$ with $\varphi_u(\lceil c\rceil, v) = \varphi_c(v)$ for all $c, v$ (both sides defined or undefined together, with the same value) and $\mathrm{runtime}(u, (\lceil c\rceil, v)) \le p\bigl(|c| + |v| + \mathrm{runtime}(c, v)\bigr)$ whenever the right-hand side is defined.

This is blueprint `lem:universal-tm` (the efficient universal Turing machine, [MNY, Lemma 2.1]), the first result of the efficient computability toolkit. It is the universal machine used by the efficient Kleene recursion theorem (`efficient_fixed_point`, blueprint `lem:kleene`) and, through it, by the recursive compression lemma; the compression pipeline's deciders use its clocked companion `exists_clocked_universal`.

**Formalization Note**: The blueprint states the bound with a polynomial in three arguments $|e|, |x|, \mathrm{runtime}(e,x)$; the Lean uses a single polynomial in their sum, which is equivalent. The structure is stated as data (program and polynomial as fields) rather than as an existential so that downstream definitions can name them; the theorem only asserts that the type is inhabited, and its witness is the self-interpreter `selfUniversal` of `Cost/Universal.lean` (program `univProg`, polynomial `univPoly` with $\mathtt{univPoly}(X) = (3X+1)(\mathtt{interpBodyBound}(\mathtt{sigmaFun}\,X) + 1) + 2X + 11$). The input is the pair $(\lceil c\rceil, v)$ encoded as $\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v$, and the sizes $|c|, |v|$ are node counts of the encodings, which are the bit-lengths of their preorder serializations.
nodes.source: https://github.com/vidick/MIPRE-formalization/blob/70cbf1c52e3d5e1dff1162fdf952c9a9f4bd99ed/MIPRE/Foundations/Cost/Universal.lean#L1537-L1538; blueprint lem:universal-tm, https://vidick.github.io/MIPRE-formalization/blueprint/; [MNY] A. Marks, S. S. Nezhadi, H. Yuen, The recursive compression method for proving undecidability results, manuscript, Lemma 2.1
nodes.explanation:
We prove that the type `UniversalMachine` is inhabited: there are a closed program $u$ and a polynomial $p$ such that every run of a program $c$ on $v$ with result $r$ and cost $t$ yields a run of $u$ on $(\lceil c\rceil, v)$ with result $r$ and cost at most $p(|c| + |v| + t)$, and every run of $u$ on $(\lceil c\rceil, v)$ with result $r$ yields a run of $c$ on $v$ with result $r$.

The witness is the self-interpreter `selfUniversal`. Its program is $u = \mathtt{univProg} = \mathsf{let}\;\mathtt{univPrelude}\;(\mathsf{loop}\;\mathtt{interpBody})$: the prelude turns the input $\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v$ into the encoding $\lceil c_0\rceil$ of the initial configuration $c_0 = \langle\mathsf{ev}\,c, [v], [\,]\rangle$ of the evaluation machine (at cost at most $|c| + |v| + 10$, `univPrelude_runs`), and the loop iterates the body, which stops with the returned value on a final configuration and otherwise replaces the configuration by its successor using the step program. Closedness is checked syntactically (`univProg_wellScoped`). The polynomial is `univPoly`, with $\mathtt{univPoly}(X) = \mathtt{univBoundFun}(X) = (3X+1)(\mathtt{interpBodyBound}(\mathtt{sigmaFun}\,X) + 1) + 2X + 11$, where $\mathtt{interpBodyBound}(S) = (S+1)(S+40) + 200 + 3S + 30$ bounds one iteration on configurations of size at most $S$ and $\mathtt{sigmaFun}(X) = \mathtt{cfgSizeBound}(X, 3X, X, 2X)$ is a cubic polynomial.

The simulation clause is `univProg_time_le`. Given a run of $c$ on $v$ with result $r$ and cost $t$, put $X = |c| + |v| + t$. The initial configuration satisfies the bound $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,X\,X\,X\,X$ (program of size $|c|$, one environment value of size $|v|$, empty stack). The imported theorem `eval_steps_bound`, in its form `eval_steps_bound_forever` (which extends it beyond the final configuration, using that final configurations are fixed), asserts that along the machine run of a derivation of cost $t \le V$ from a configuration bounded by $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,V\,L\,P\,K$, every configuration is bounded by $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,V\,(L+2t)\,P\,(K+t)$: here by $\mathtt{CfgBound}\,X\,(3X)\,X\,(2X)$. The imported theorem `size_toData_le` turns this into $\mathrm{size}\lceil\mathsf{step}^{n}(c_0)\rceil \le \mathtt{sigmaFun}(X)$ for all $n$. The imported theorem `eval_steps_count` asserts that the derivation corresponds to a machine run of some $N \le 3t$ steps from $c_0$ to a final configuration with value $r$. The imported theorem `interpLoop_runs`, applied with $S = \mathtt{sigmaFun}(X)$, this $N$, $n = 0$ and $m = N$, gives a run of the loop from $\lceil c_0\rceil$ (above the input in the environment) with result $r$ at cost at most $(N+1)(\mathtt{interpBodyBound}(S)+1) \le (3X+1)(\mathtt{interpBodyBound}(S)+1)$. The $\mathsf{let}$ rule combines prelude and loop, adding one unit, for a total within $\mathtt{univBoundFun}(X)$.

The no-spurious-halting clause is `univProg_halts_of`. A run of $u$ on $\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v$ with result $r$ is a $\mathsf{let}$ derivation: a run of the prelude with some value $w$, followed by a run of the loop from $w$. The imported theorem `Eval.deterministic` (two runs of the same program in the same environment have the same result and cost), compared with the hand-built prelude run, gives $w = \lceil c_0\rceil$. The imported theorem `interpLoop_rev` asserts that a halting run of the interpreter loop from $\lceil c\rceil$ with result $r$ comes from a machine run reaching a final configuration with value $r$: so $\mathsf{step}^{N}(c_0) = \langle\mathsf{ret}\,r, e, [\,]\rangle$ for some $N, e$. Finally the imported theorem `halts_iff` asserts that $c$ halts on $v$ with result $r$ if and only if the machine run from $c_0$ reaches a final configuration with value $r$; its backward direction, which extracts a derivation from the machine run (`eval_of_steps`) and uses that final configurations are fixed to see that the derivation's result is $r$, gives a cost $t$ with $\mathsf{Eval}\;[v]\;c\;r\;t$.

The theorem itself is the one-line packaging $\langle\mathtt{selfUniversal}\rangle$ of these five fields, the polynomial bound being transported from $\mathtt{univBoundFun}$ to $\mathtt{univPoly}$ by the evaluation identity `univPoly_eval`.

nodes.theorem_title: Existence of a clocked universal machine: total, budgeted simulation in polynomial time
nodes.natural_language_statement:
Fix the ambient cost model: programs $c$ run on values $v$ (binary trees), $\mathsf{Eval}\;[v]\;c\;r\;t$ (`c.Runs v r t`) says that $c$ halts on $v$ with result $r$ at cost $t$, programs are encoded as values $\lceil c\rceil$ of size $|c|$, and budgets are passed in unary, $\mathsf{ofNat}(k)$ being the list of $k$ copies of $\mathsf{nil}$. The *budgeted result* of $c$ on $v$ under the cost budget $k$ is
$$ \mathtt{clockedResult}(c, v, k) = \begin{cases} \mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\mathsf{nil}\,\mathsf{nil})\,r & \text{if } c \text{ halts on } v \text{ with result } r \text{ at some cost } t \le k, \\ \mathsf{nil} & \text{otherwise (timeout)}. \end{cases} $$

A *clocked universal machine* (`ClockedUniversalMachine`) is a structure consisting of a closed program $u_T$ (reading only its input) and a polynomial $p \in \mathbb{N}[X]$ such that for every program $c$, every input $v$ and every budget $k \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a cost
$$ t \le p\bigl(k + |c| + |v|\bigr) \quad\text{with}\quad \mathsf{Eval}\;\bigl[\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{ofNat}\,k)\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v)\bigr]\;u_T\;\mathtt{clockedResult}(c, v, k)\;t . $$
The theorem states that such a machine exists:
$$ \mathsf{Nonempty}\;\mathtt{ClockedUniversalMachine} . $$

In words: there is a fixed program that, given $k$, a program $c$ and an input $v$, runs $c$ on $v$ for cost at most $k$ and reports either the result or a timeout, always halting, and does so in time polynomial in $k + |c| + |v|$. This is the time-bounded half of blueprint `lem:universal-tm` (efficient universal Turing machine, [MNY, Lemma 2.1]). It is the primitive with which the deciders of the compression pipeline (introspection, parallel repetition) simulate other deciders under a budget, and with which the recursive compression argument runs a description $e$ "for $\log n$ steps"; because the machine is a structure, downstream definitions can refer to its program and its overhead polynomial as data.

**Formalization Note**: The budget $k$ counts cost units of the big-step semantics and is given in unary, so a polynomial bound in $k$ is the appropriate notion ("run for $k$ steps" with $k$ written out); the input is the triple encoded as $\mathsf{cons}\,(\mathsf{ofNat}\,k)\,(\mathsf{cons}\,\lceil c\rceil\,v)$. The witness is the clocked self-interpreter `selfClockedUniversal` of `Cost/Universal.lean` (program `univTProg`, polynomial `univTPoly`). The result is total, which the blueprint statement of `lem:universal-tm` does not mention separately: it covers the unclocked machine, and the clocked variant is attached to the same blueprint node.
